2.text: and sometimes are ornamented with geometrical designs scratched in with a

3.text: knife or impressed in the soft bark with sharp stamps. The Chukchee use

4.text: these boxes for holding snuff, chewing-tobacco, and any small objects which

5.text: they are afraid of losing. Occasionally a lump of sugar gets in with the mixture,

6.text: and its sweetness is improved, to their taste, by the additional tobacco flavor.

7.text: The Koryak, the Kerek, the Russianized Yukaghir, and also the Chukchee

8.text: of the Kolyma, make snuff-boxes of the same styles, using wood, antler, and

9.text: ivory. The same is true of the Alaskan Eskimo. Many of the shapes rep-

10.text: resented by Nelson¹ have their counterparts in Asia.
10.note: Footnote marker keyed as superscript U+00B9, per §2.10; anchors the note on line 43.

11.text: I have met men and women who used tobacco in all three ways at the

12.text: same time. Usually, however, snuff is only used when smoking cannot be

13.text: continued because it causes a cough, or for some other reason. Taking snuff

14.text: is considered a cure for rheum, weakness of the eyes, and even dulness of

15.text: hearing. In the Kolyma region, smoking and chewing are of equal impor-

16.text: tance, but on the Pacific chewing is much more general.

17.text: INTOXICANTS. — Fly-agaric is the only means of intoxication discovered
17.note: Run-in second-level heading set in small capitals; keyed plain ASCII capitals per §2.13.

18.text: by the natives of northeastern Asia. Its use is more common in the Koryak

19.text: tribe, as agaric does not grow outside of the forest border. For the same
19.note: A small mid-height ink speck sits between 'of' and 'the' at roughly 60% of the line width (zoomed at 2x). Not a hyphen or any catalogued mark; ruled a print artifact and not keyed.

20.text: reason only the Southern Pacific Chukchee — e. g., those around the Anadyr,

21.text: Big River, and Opuka River — are supplied with the intoxicating mushroom.

22.text: They do not compare with the Koryak, however, in their passion for agaric.

23.text: The Russianized natives of the Anadyr until recently shared in the con-

24.text: sumption of this intoxicant, but now they have almost wholly given up its use.

25.text: The reason of this change is that they consider the strong intoxication produced

26.text: by this stimulant as shameful for a Christian. They also realize that the

27.text: consumption of fly-agaric involves some danger. With a person unaccustomed

28.text: to its use it may even cause death. The abstinence from agaric is also noticed

29.text: among the northern Kamchadal, and to some degree among the Maritime

30.text: Koryak of northern Kamchatka, though all of these people gather it assiduously

31.text: in order to trade it to their less civilized reindeer-breeding neighbors.

32.text: Fortunately for the tribes consuming the fly-agaric, it grows only in cer-

33.text: tain places, and the supply is often limited. The mushrooms are usually

34.text: dried up and strung together in threes, that number being an average dose.

35.text: Some of the natives of course require much more to produce any effect. The

36.text: intoxication may be followed by sickness, or the after-effect may be very slight.

37.text: When eaten, the mushrooms are torn to small shreds, and these are chewed

38.text: piece by piece, and swallowed with a little water. Among the Koryak the

39.text: woman chews the mushroom, and offers the ready quid to her husband to swallow.

40.text: I witnessed a few times the progress of intoxication by means of agaric.

41.text: The symptoms are analogous to those produced by opium or hasheesh. The

42.text: intoxication comes on rather suddenly, in about a quarter of an hour after
